heading: Host names and local addresses
body:
`ty preview`, `ty serve` and `ty start` bind `127.0.0.1` unless you choose another address. A server on a loopback address answers a request only when its `Host` name is `localhost`, a name under `.localhost`, an IP address, the host of `tac.origin`, or a name in `server.hosts` in `server/application.json`. Any other name gets `403` with `TY1366`, and a `Host` that the server cannot read gets `400`. This stops DNS rebinding: a web page on another name points its name at your computer, and the browser then lets the page read your local app as if the app were its own. Because the page still sends its own name, the server refuses it, in every browser. The check runs before routing, so it covers pages, controller routes, the hot-update stream and WebSocket upgrades. It reads `Host` itself and ignores `X-Forwarded-Host`. A server opened to the network with `--allow-non-loopback` checks `Host` only when `server.hosts` is set, so a reverse proxy keeps working; set `server.hosts` there too.

Yon code reaches a local service only through a name or address in `outgoing.hosts`. A localhost name such as `api.localhost`, or `*.localhost` for every such name, reaches `[::1]` and then `127.0.0.1` on every operating system: the guard answers the name itself and ignores `/etc/hosts`. This works for the clients that read the proxy settings: JavaScript and TypeScript, Python, Ruby, PHP with cURL, Go, C# and Rust with reqwest. The Java, Groovy, Kotlin and Dart default clients read them only when you ask them to (`ProxySelector.getDefault()`, `HttpClient.findProxyFromEnvironment`). On macOS and Linux the operating system also confines every handler process, the programs it starts and every Gateway command (ADR 0113): it can connect only to the guard and to its server's resource port on loopback, so UDP, DNS lookups, other loopback ports and every other address are refused. So a client that does not use the guard, or a raw socket, cannot reach anything. `ty start` refuses to start with `TY2113` when it cannot apply this confinement, for example on Windows or on Linux older than 6.7; where the platform already limits egress, set `YON_EGRESS_ENFORCEMENT=proxy` in the environment of `ty`. `ty serve` and `ty preview` start anyway and log `handler.egress_unenforced`.

The guard resolves an allowed name once and connects to that address. It refuses a name that resolves only to loopback, private, link-local (such as the cloud metadata address `169.254.169.254`) or shared addresses. So an allowed wildcard such as `*.example.com` cannot be pointed at your own services. To reach a private service, list its IP address. While the guard runs, handler processes get no `NO_PROXY`, so no client can go around it, and Go's standard client sends its requests to the guard too. ADR 0094 explains the choices.
